title: Genetic Engineering
description: A radio debate about gene editing in medicine, farming and the environment, with a farmer calling in and a closing discussion of the ethics of enhancement.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · The case for editing genes
parts.intro: You will hear the presenter of a radio debate, Claire, questioning Professor Dalton, who supports genetic engineering.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: Welcome to Open Question. Tonight's motion is that humanity should embrace genetic engineering. Professor Dalton, you're for it, and you've asked to begin with a patient.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: I have. A few years ago I met a girl of eight with a severe inherited blood disorder. Her life had been a cycle of hospital visits and transfusions. Today, after treatment that edits her own cells, she is playing football. That is not a distant promise. It's something that has already happened.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: Powerful. But critics would say one success story is not a policy.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: Agreed, and I wouldn't pretend otherwise. The point of the story is the principle. We have long accepted that doctors may alter the body to heal it, with drugs, with surgery, with transplants. Editing a faulty gene in a sick person is the same moral act performed with a sharper tool.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: Though the tool is permanent, isn't it? A drug wears off.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: For the patient, yes, and that's exactly what makes it valuable for a disease that would otherwise last a lifetime. The permanence is a reason to be careful, but not a reason to refuse. We accept the permanence of a hip replacement.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: What about the cost? These treatments run into hundreds of thousands.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: A serious problem, and I'll be blunt: if only the rich benefit, then the technology will have failed, ethically if not scientifically. But expensive first-generation treatments have usually become affordable, and that argues for investment and fair pricing, not for a ban.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: We'll test that claim later in the programme, but first I'd like to bring in a second voice, because I suspect Dr Nguyen has been waiting patiently.

parts.title: Part 2 · Ecosystems and gene drives
parts.intro: You will hear Dr Nguyen, who opposes the motion, debating with Professor Dalton about engineered insects.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Professor, I have no quarrel with the girl. My concern is what happens when we move from patients, who consent, to ecosystems, which can't. Take the proposal to release mosquitoes engineered to spread a gene that makes their offspring sterile, so an entire species could disappear from a region.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: A proposal that could save hundreds of thousands of lives a year from malaria. Surely you wouldn't dismiss that?

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: I wouldn't dismiss it, but I'd ask who decides. A mosquito doesn't respect borders. If one country releases them, its neighbours inherit the consequences without a vote.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: Fair, though we already share rivers, air and fish stocks across borders. The answer is international governance, with staged trials, starting on islands where the animals can be contained.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: On paper, yes. In practice, the track record of international agreements on shared environments is, shall we say, mixed. And there's the biology. Species are knotted into food webs in ways we only partly understand. Remove one insect, and something else may flourish in its place.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: Which is why trials come first. Ignorance cuts both ways, though. We don't fully understand the consequences of leaving the disease alone either, and those consequences are well documented. Children are dying.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: I don't deny that. My point is about irreversibility. If a trial of a medicine fails, we stop giving the medicine. If a self-spreading genetic change goes wrong, there may be no way to recall it.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: I accept that irreversibility changes the calculation, which is why I'd want a way to reverse it built in at the start.

parts.title: Part 3 · A farmer calls in
parts.intro: You will hear Claire taking a call from a rice farmer, Mr Hoang.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: We have a caller, Mr Hoang, who grows rice in the Mekong delta. Go ahead, Mr Hoang.

script.speaker: Mr Hoang
script.text: Thank you. I've been farming for thirty years, and I want to say something that neither of your guests has said. For me, this is not abstract. Last year, salt water from the sea crept into my fields and destroyed half my harvest. We borrowed money to get through the winter, and we are still paying it back.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: I'm sorry to hear that. That must have been a very frightening season for you and your family.

script.speaker: Mr Hoang
script.text: A neighbour planted a salt-tolerant variety and lost almost nothing. It was developed by scientists using modern methods. My family had been sceptical, I'll admit. We thought it was unnatural. But when you are watching your income vanish, the word natural doesn't pay for school fees.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: Some argue that these varieties tie farmers to big companies who own the seeds.

script.speaker: Mr Hoang
script.text: That is a legitimate worry, and I share it. The variety my neighbour used came from a public research institute, and the seeds were free to save and replant. That's the model I'd like to see. If the seeds are locked up by a few firms, then I'd be against it as well. The problem is not the science, it's who owns it.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: So your position is closer to conditional support.

script.speaker: Mr Hoang
script.text: Yes, but I'd say a fairly firm one. I've been left behind by the weather enough times. I don't want to be left behind by the laboratory too.

script.speaker: Claire
script.text: Thank you, Mr Hoang. A reminder that the people most affected are often not in the studio.

parts.title: Part 4 · Therapy, enhancement and rules
parts.intro: You will hear Dr Nguyen and Professor Dalton make their closing arguments.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Let me turn to the question I think matters most. Healing disease is one thing. But the same tools could, in principle, be used to select the height, intelligence or appearance of children. Where does therapy end and enhancement begin?

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: A line that's hard to draw, I admit. Is it therapy to protect a child from a gene that raises the risk of heart disease? Most would say yes. And what about a gene that improves memory in old age?

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Exactly. Each step looks reasonable, and yet the sum is a world in which parents feel obliged to optimise their children, and in which those who can't afford it fall behind. I worry about a quiet inequality hardening into biology.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: That worry is serious, but note that we already have inequality in education, nutrition and healthcare, and we don't conclude that nutrition should be banned. We try to widen access. I would say the same here.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: Widening access to a treatment for illness, yes. But enhancement is different, because there is no natural stopping point. The goalposts move.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: Then let's draw rules. Many countries already prohibit changes that would be inherited by future generations, except in strictly controlled research. I'd support keeping that line for now, while the technology is young, and reviewing it as evidence accumulates.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: That's rather closer to my position than I expected, I must say.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: I'm in favour of the technology, not of recklessness. The sceptics have done us a service by forcing us to say what we'd refuse.

script.speaker: Dr Nguyen
script.text: And the enthusiasts have reminded us that refusing to act is also a choice with victims.

script.speaker: Professor Dalton
script.text: Perhaps that is as good a conclusion as a debate can produce.

questions.text: Why does Professor Dalton begin with the story of the girl?
options: To argue that children should always be treated first
To show that hospitals are too expensive for most families to use
To prove that football helps patients to recover faster
To show that gene editing already works, not just in theory
questions.explanation: He says her recovery is not a distant promise but something that has already happened.

evidence.quote: That is not a distant promise.

questions.text: How does Professor Dalton compare gene editing with other medicine?
options: It is more dangerous than surgery because it is permanent
It is a completely new moral problem with no precedent
It is morally like other treatments, but with a sharper tool
It is less ethical than drugs because it alters the body
questions.explanation: He says editing a faulty gene is the same moral act as drugs, surgery or transplants, performed with a sharper tool.

evidence.quote: the same moral act performed with a sharper tool

questions.text: What is Professor Dalton's view of the permanence of gene editing?
options: It is the main reason why it should be banned outright
It is unimportant for patients with lifelong diseases
It is a serious problem that has no solution at all
It calls for care but is not a reason to refuse treatment
questions.explanation: He says permanence is a reason to be careful but not to refuse, and compares it to a hip replacement.

evidence.quote: The permanence is a reason to be careful, but not a reason to refuse.

questions.text: How does Professor Dalton respond to the question of cost?
options: He suggests that only the rich should receive treatment at first
He claims that the cost of treatment is not important
He says prices will fall without any need for action
He accepts it is serious and would call unfair access a failure
questions.explanation: He calls it a serious problem and says that if only the rich benefit, the technology will have failed ethically.

evidence.quote: if only the rich benefit, then the technology will have failed

questions.text: What is Claire's objection to the story of the girl?
options: The treatment was unsafe for children of that age
The girl was too young to give her consent
One success does not justify a general policy
The story had not been proved to be true
questions.explanation: She says critics would argue one success story is not a policy.

evidence.quote: one success story is not a policy

questions.text: What distinction does Dr Nguyen draw at the start?
options: Insects are more dangerous than humans
Doctors are more careful than farmers
Patients can consent, but ecosystems cannot
Girls respond better than adults to gene editing
questions.explanation: She says her concern is moving from patients, who consent, to ecosystems, which can't.

evidence.quote: patients, who consent, to ecosystems, which can't

questions.text: Why does Dr Nguyen say a mosquito does not respect borders?
options: Governments would not allow such releases to happen
Borders between countries are often poorly marked
Neighbours could suffer the consequences without a vote
Mosquitoes are impossible to count or to track accurately
questions.explanation: She explains that if one country releases the insects, its neighbours inherit the consequences without a vote.

evidence.quote: its neighbours inherit the consequences without a vote

questions.text: What does Dr Nguyen think of international agreements on shared environments?
options: She thinks they are unnecessary for shared rivers
She wants them to be much stronger than they are
She doubts that they work well in practice
She believes they are completely reliable in practice
questions.explanation: She says the track record is mixed, so she is sceptical that governance on paper would work in practice.

evidence.quote: the track record of international agreements on shared environments is, shall we say, mixed

questions.text: Why does Professor Dalton say that ignorance cuts both ways?
options: To argue that doing nothing also has serious, known results
To suggest that trials are unnecessary before any release occurs
To admit that scientists know very little about insects
To show that malaria is not very dangerous after all
questions.explanation: He says we also do not fully understand what happens if we leave the disease alone, though its consequences are well documented.

evidence.quote: Ignorance cuts both ways, though.

questions.text: What does Professor Dalton concede at the end of the exchange?
options: Irreversibility matters, so a way to reverse it should be built in
The trials should be cancelled until the law is clear
Neighbouring countries should have a vote before any release
Mosquitoes should never be released under any conditions
questions.explanation: He accepts that irreversibility changes the calculation and says he would want a built-in way to reverse it.

evidence.quote: a way to reverse it built in at the start

questions.text: What happened to Mr Hoang's rice harvest last year?
options: A neighbour's crop spread disease to it
Drought reduced it slightly
Salt water destroyed half of it
The seeds failed to grow
questions.explanation: He says salt water from the sea crept into his fields and destroyed half his harvest.

evidence.quote: destroyed half my harvest

questions.text: What does Mr Hoang mean by the word natural does not pay for school fees?
options: Natural crops are always more profitable for farmers
Practical needs matter more to him than being natural
He has given up farming because of the debts
Schools are too expensive for most rice farmers
questions.explanation: He says his family thought modified rice was unnatural, but watching his income vanish changed his priorities.

evidence.quote: the word natural doesn't pay for school fees

questions.text: Under what condition would Mr Hoang oppose modified seeds?
options: If the seeds could tolerate salt
If the variety came from a neighbour
If a few firms control the seeds
If the seeds were developed by scientists
questions.explanation: He says that if the seeds are locked up by a few firms he would be against it, because the problem is who owns it.

evidence.quote: If the seeds are locked up by a few firms

questions.text: How would Mr Hoang describe his own position?
options: Fairly firm support, with conditions about ownership
Total support with no conditions about who owns seeds
Complete opposition to modified crops of any kind
Uncertainty about whether the science really works
questions.explanation: Claire calls it conditional support, and he agrees that it is fairly firm.

evidence.quote: Yes, but I'd say a fairly firm one.

questions.text: What is the purpose of Claire's final comment?
options: To criticise the caller's views on modern breeding methods and seeds
To end the call politely without further comment
To suggest that farmers should join the studio panel
To note that those most affected are often absent from debates
questions.explanation: She calls the caller a reminder that the people most affected are often not in the studio.

evidence.quote: the people most affected are often not in the studio

questions.text: Why does Dr Nguyen ask where therapy ends and enhancement begins?
options: To ask the professor for his personal opinion on it
To suggest the line between them is hard to draw
To change the subject to education and nutrition
To prove that therapy is wrong in all cases
questions.explanation: She introduces the problem that the same tools could be used to select traits, so it is unclear where healing stops.

evidence.quote: Where does therapy end and enhancement begin?

questions.text: What is Dr Nguyen's main worry about enhancement?
options: The enormous cost of research for national governments
The loss of interest in education among young people
The risk of serious mistakes in the laboratory itself
Pressure on parents and inequality becoming fixed in biology
questions.explanation: She worries that parents would feel obliged to optimise their children and those who cannot afford it would fall behind.

evidence.quote: a quiet inequality hardening into biology

questions.text: How does Professor Dalton answer the worry about inequality?
options: He claims that nutrition is more important than genes
He suggests banning all forms of enhancement for now
He says inequality exists elsewhere and access should widen
He says that inequality is unavoidable and cannot change
questions.explanation: He compares it to education, nutrition and healthcare, where we try to widen access rather than ban them.

evidence.quote: We try to widen access.

questions.text: Which rule does Professor Dalton support for now?
options: Freedom for parents to choose any changes they like
A ban on inheritable changes outside controlled research
A law that bans every kind of enhancement forever
A ban on all gene editing, even for patients
questions.explanation: He supports keeping the existing prohibition on changes inherited by future generations, apart from controlled research.

evidence.quote: Many countries already prohibit changes that would be inherited by future generations

questions.text: What do the speakers agree on at the end?
options: Gene editing should be banned until the cost falls
Debates like this one never reach any conclusions
Both caution and action are needed, since inaction has victims
Scientists should decide the rules entirely alone
questions.explanation: Dr Nguyen says refusing to act is a choice with victims, and Professor Dalton says sceptics forced them to say what they would refuse.

evidence.quote: refusing to act is also a choice with victims
